lessons.title: ਕਿ (ki) — that
lessons.gloss: that — one sihari away from the word for what

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: From the chapter behind you, the two words for but. And from the naming lesson, the word for what.

segments.instruction: par, lekin — then ਕੀ
ate — from two chapters back

segments.text: Look at these two very carefully, because they are not the same word:
ਕੀ — kī — what, with the long bihari.
ਕਿ — ki — that, with the short sihari.
One stroke apart, and completely different jobs. You have had ਕੀ since you first asked someone's name. ਕਿ (ki) is new.
ਅਤੇ and ਪਰ put two sentences side by side. ਕਿ (ki) does something different: it lets one sentence be swallowed by another, as the thing a verb is about.
(verb of thinking, knowing or saying) ਕਿ (whole sentence).
English does the same with that, and like English, Punjabi often drops it in speech. Learn it in place first.

segments.instruction: kī and ki — long, then short. Say them until they separate.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: *kī* and *ki* — long, then short. Say them until they separate.]

segments.instruction: ki, then any sentence you own, after it.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ki*, then any sentence you own, after it.]

segments.instruction: two sentences joined by ate, then one swallowed by ki.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: two sentences joined by *ate*, then one swallowed by *ki*.]

segments.text: What separates ਕਿ (ki) from ਕੀ, in writing and in meaning? (One stroke — sihari against bihari; that against what.)

lessons.title: ਮੈਂ ਸੋਚਦਾ ਹਾਂ ਕਿ (maiṁ sochdā hāṁ ki) — I think that…
lessons.gloss: I think that... - the frame an opinion travels in

segments.text: One lesson back, the swallowing word. And from the lesson that gave you ਮੈਂ, the word for I and the copula that follows it.

segments.instruction: ki, and maiṁ … hāṁ
ate joining two sentences — from two chapters back
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: *ate* joining two sentences — from two chapters back]

segments.text: ਮੈਂ ਸੋਚਦਾ ਹਾਂ ਕਿ … — maiṁ sochdā hāṁ ki … — "I think that …"
Three of the four pieces are old: ਮੈਂ, the habitual ending you met with bolda, and ਹਾਂ. Only ਕਿ (ki) is new, and it opens the space your opinion goes into.
A woman says ਸੋਚਦੀ — sochdī — with the feminine ending, exactly as with every habitual verb this book has taught. The sentence you use is the one that matches you.

Everything you can already say can now be said as an opinion rather than as a fact. That is a large change for one small word, and it is the difference between reporting the world and having a view about it.

segments.instruction: the frame, in the form that matches you, and finish it.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the frame, in the form that matches you, and finish it.]

segments.instruction: a bare sentence, then the same one inside the frame.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: a bare sentence, then the same one inside the frame.]

segments.instruction: an opinion whose inside half is negative.
segments.source: [YOU BUILD: an opinion whose inside half is negative.]

segments.text: Give an opinion about anything you can name. Which piece of the frame was new today? (Only ਕਿ (ki).)

lessons.title: ਕਿ (ki) reaches the page
lessons.gloss: that, on the page — and the one stroke that separates it from what

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
waitUntilStopped: Script — one stroke is the whole lesson
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script — one stroke is the whole lesson until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: One chapter back you wrote ਪਰ, standing alone. Write it once from memory.

blocks.title: Script — one stroke is the whole lesson

segments.text: Uncover both and put them side by side:
ਕਿ (ki) — the short ਿ sihari, written before the letter.
ਕੀ — the long ੀ bihari, written after it.

Same consonant. The vowel stroke sits on a different side, and that alone is the difference between that and what. Both signs have been yours for many chapters; what is new is that the pair now matters.

blocks.title: Writing — guided copy, model in view

segments.text: Copy ਕਿ (ki) once with the model in view, then ਕੀ beneath it. Check which side each stroke fell on before you go on.
Write both. Which one is that, and how does its stroke sit? (ਕਿ (ki) — the sihari, before the letter.)

segments.instruction: ਅਤੇ written — from two chapters back
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: **ਅਤੇ** written — from two chapters back]

lessons.title: ਕਿਉਂ (kyoṁ) — why
lessons.gloss: why - the one member of the k- family this book never named

segments.text: One lesson back you wrote ਕਿ (ki). And from the wellbeing lesson, the question word that taught you the family they all belong to.

segments.instruction: ਕਿ, and kivēṁ — every question word opens with ਕ
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: **ਕਿ**, and *kivēṁ* — every question word opens with **ਕ**]

segments.instruction: jāṁ — from two chapters back

segments.text: ਕਿਉਂ — kyoṁ — why.

The same ਕ as every question word in the family. This one has been missing: the book named the family when it taught kivēṁ, listed its members, and ਕਿਉਂ (kyoṁ) was the one it left out — so a reader could ask several things and never why.
That is not a small omission. Why is the question that asks for a reason, and the next lesson is the word that answers it.

segments.instruction: kyoṁ? — flat, as a whole question.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *kyoṁ?* — flat, as a whole question.]

segments.instruction: kivēṁ? and kyoṁ? — how, and why.
the family's shared opening ਕ, then kyoṁ.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the family's shared opening **ਕ**, then *kyoṁ*.]

segments.text: Ask why. What do every question word in this family share, and where were you first told so? (The opening ਕ; the kivēṁ lesson.)

lessons.title: ਕਿਉਂਕਿ (kyoṁki) — because
lessons.gloss: because - the question word with the swallowing word stuck to it

segments.text: The two words this chapter has already given you.

segments.instruction: kyoṁ, and ki
nā … nā … — from two chapters back
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: *nā … nā …* — from two chapters back]

segments.text: The answer is the question with the swallowing word stuck to the end of it:
ਕਿਉਂ (why) + ਕਿ (that) = ਕਿਉਂਕਿ (kyoṁki) — because.
Both halves are already yours from earlier in this chapter; the join is the only new thing. Punjabi answers why by saying, in effect, "why-that", and the reason then follows as a whole sentence.
(what happened) ਕਿਉਂਕਿ (kyoṁki) (the reason).
Note the ਕਿ (ki) at the end is the short sihari one — the that you learned, not the what. Reading the word slowly is its own revision of the pair.

segments.instruction: kyoṁ — then kyoṁki. The question, then the answer's opening.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *kyoṁ* — then *kyoṁki*. The question, then the answer's opening.]

segments.instruction: any sentence, kyoṁki, and a reason.
segments.source: [YOU BUILD: any sentence, *kyoṁki*, and a reason.]

segments.instruction: ask kyoṁ? and answer yourself.

segments.text: Ask why, then answer it. What two words is ਕਿਉਂਕਿ (kyoṁki) built from, and which ਕਿ is on the end? (ਕਿਉਂ and ਕਿ; the short sihari that.) Next chapter: if, and when.
